summary:
Washington stands under the United States federal framework, which governs travel documents and entry screening in every state. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and a State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 bar visas for trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flag applicants under the internal code SWS25, and allow an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth to be treated as fraud and permanently barred.

Checkpoint screening carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded: in April 2025 CNN reported that multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are tightening elsewhere. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Washington's own legal position is materially different from the states above. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment names Washington among the "Most Protective" states, and groups it with Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland as states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, alongside refugee protections for people fleeing hostile states.

Washington has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and appears on a nationwide tracker of such measures. For people held in state custody, Washington prisons were legally required as of October 2023, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, documenting birth-sex housing used as a sanction in 2024.

Two November ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, are flagged by the July 2026 assessment as targeting transgender residents of Washington.
